content: I printed the modified wiper base for the extended purge bin out of PCCF before dismantling my Core One for the upgrade and discovered now that the silicone wiper and priming block are very difficult to insert. Thankfully silicone parts can take a lot of abuse without any damage, so I used the largest allen key to basically push/squeeze and pack in the edges of the silicone parts deep into the receptacles using lots of force until the holes finally lined up.
wording: sloped side is not a direction. the lower side towards the middle
my factory built core one + didn't even come with this screwdriver... annoying...

Why do these need to be torx head screws? And then with such tiny screwdriver passthrough holes? Seriously, was the goal to go out of the way to make assembly as miserable as possible if you didn't save all the tools that came with the printer?
I cracked the slot for the wiper while securing the srew. It cracked along the layer line. I used very minimal force. Could be enforced by a millimeter or os.

replies.content: Same for me.  Cautious reminder to others.  Just lightly snug this thing up

content: I did not understand the picture of how to insert the wiper in the base; make sure that the base is in line with the 2 holes, rather than having a few millimetres difference between the wiper hole and the base, if they don't align, turn it around
It’d be nice if the Wiper-base had slightly larger cutouts to accommodate screwdrivers other than the Prusa one

replies.content: So much this. For the people designing this stuff - if it's that dependent on a very specific tool that probably costs you a dime, JUST INCLUDE THE TOOL. Not everyone saved every single random allen/torx wrench that came with their printer, especially if they got it pre-assembled and literally never had a use for them before now.
